hook.text: A virus that kills cancer — oncolytic viruses infect tumor cells and burst them open while sparing healthy tissue.

buildup.text: Viruses are engineered to replicate only inside cancer cells — mutations disable their growth in normal tissue.

discovery.text: T-VEC is an approved herpes virus that destroys melanoma — it also releases signals that recruit the immune system.

twist.text: The immune system often clears the virus before it reaches distant tumors — delivery remains a major barrier.

climax.text: Combining oncolytic viruses with checkpoint inhibitors boosts response rates — the virus primes what immunotherapy finishes.

punchline.text: Fight fire with fire — oncolytic viruses turn infections into cancer cures.

quiz.question: How does T-VEC treat melanoma?
options: It blocks blood supply to melanoma tumors
It is an engineered herpes virus that selectively infects and destroys melanoma cells while stimulating immune response
It delivers chemotherapy drugs directly inside cancer cells

details.summary: Oncolytic virus therapy uses engineered viruses that selectively infect and kill cancer cells while sparing normal tissue. The viruses replicate inside tumors, destroying them from within and stimulating anti-tumor immune responses that attack distant metastases.
details.whyItMatters: Oncolytic viruses turn a patient's tumor into its own vaccine factory. By destroying cancer cells and exposing tumor antigens to the immune system, they combine direct killing with immunotherapy, offering a unique dual mechanism of action.
takeaways: Oncolytic viruses selectively infect and replicate in cancer cells
Tumor destruction releases antigens that stimulate anti-tumor immunity
T-VEC was the first FDA-approved oncolytic virus therapy in 2015

faq.question: How do oncolytic viruses selectively kill cancer cells?
faq.answer: Cancer cells often have disabled antiviral defenses that normal cells retain. Oncolytic viruses are engineered to exploit these defects, replicating freely in cancer cells while being contained by normal cells' intact interferon responses. Tumor-specific promoters add additional selectivity.

faq.question: Can oncolytic viruses spread to other people?
faq.answer: Approved oncolytic viruses are engineered with safety features preventing efficient transmission. They are attenuated and cannot replicate well outside tumor cells. While shedding can occur, the virus cannot cause disease in healthy individuals.
